documents.title: ECTRIMS EAN guideline on the pharmacological treatment of people with multiple sclerosis

chunks.content: Introduction Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a heterogenous disease, with a wide spectrum of phenotypes and highly variable disease course and treatment response [ , ]. Numerous disease modifying therapies (DMTs) are available to reduce the relapse risk and slow disability progression [ – ]. However, identifying an optimal treatment regimen often involves a stepwise, time-consuming process, frequently requiring treatment switches due to a lack of clear guidance on DMT selection [ , , – ]. One contributing issue is that guidelines classify DMT efficacy inconsistently [ , ]. For example, the German Society of Neurology (Deutsche Gesellschaft für Neurologie; DGN) groups approved DMTs into three efficacy categories based on the relative relapse reduction versus placebo: 30–50% (category 1; low efficacy), 50–60% (category 2; moderate efficacy), and > 60% (category 3; high efficacy) [ ]. Current guidelines broadly recommend initiating DMT in patients with relapsing MS (RMS) [ – ], a subtype of MS characterised by periods of new and fluctuating symptoms (relapses) [ ]. Early introduction of DMTs for patients with RMS is advised [ , ]; however, the choice and timing of DMT must be tailored to individual patient factors. Therefore, more studies are needed to better understand unmet medical needs in MS subpopulations, which may support more optimal and personalised treatment decisions. No single therapy is effective for all facets of MS, so a patient-centred treatment approach is emphasised in management guidelines [ , ]. Currently, there are no routinely used predictive biomarkers to guide the choice of a specific DMT. Treatment decisions, therefore, largely rely on clinical judgement, whereby physicians weigh expected benefits against potential safety risks for each patient. Adapting treatment to fit individuals’ medical needs and circumstances can improve prognosis, treatment adherence, outcomes, and quality of life (QoL) [ – ]. Clinicians should evaluate disease presentation and consider patient preferences (e.g., lifestyle and route/frequency of administration), as well as practical factors like cost, tolerability and, importantly, treatment effectiveness [ , ]. Shared decision-making and open dialogue between patients and healthcare professionals/physicians are crucial for aligning treatment with patient goals. Longitudinal real-world studies of MS cohorts can provide valuable insights into disease phenotypes and treatment responses in specific patient subgroups [ , ]. Leveraging such data to develop clinical patient profiles is essential to further understanding of individual disease courses and treatment responses, prerequisites for a more tailored, patient-centred approach to MS treatment [ , ]. This prospective, non-interventional cohort study PROFILE RMS (ML39348) characterised predefined patient profiles in RMS by evaluating real-world data on treatment response, disease activity, patient-reported outcomes (PROs), and safety. These profiles were defined according to unmet medical needs, namely factors prompting a treatment switch such as disease severity/activity, drug safety profile, and patient characteristics/comorbidities [ ]. Accordingly, we present 12-month follow-up data for three profiles of patients with RMS receiving DMTs: those with ongoing disease activity (Profile 1), with significant adverse drug reactions (ADRs; Profile 2), and with low treatment satisfaction (Profile 3). Methods Study design PROFILE RMS is a multicentre, prospective, observational, non-interventional study (NIS) with primary data collection from 66 centres across Germany. The study design was approved by the ethics committee of the Dresden University of Technology (EK 170042017). The first patient entered the study on July 5, 2018, and the database was locked on January 31, 2023. During a 12 month prospective observational period, assessments were performed and data collected at four timepoints corresponding to routine clinical practice: a screening visit and visits at month 0, month 6, and month 12. Assessments were collected between July 5, 2018, and September 29, 2022. A subset of safety data, specifically ADRs, were collected retrospectively 12 months prior to the study start for patients in Profile 2 (further details are provided in the procedures/assessment section below). Patients All patients signed informed consent before enrolment. Eligible patients were ≥ 18 years of age and had a diagnosis of RMS (relapsing remitting MS [RRMS] or relapsing secondary progressive MS [rSPMS]) according to the revised McDonald 2010 criteria [ ]. Patients were eligible if they belonged to one of the following treatment subgroups: patients being treated with an approved DMT (glatiramer acetate, interferon beta, dimethyl fumarate, teriflunomide, fingolimod, alemtuzumab, natalizumab, cladribine, mitoxantrone, or ocrelizumab), patients not currently being treated, and patients who were treatment-naïve. Patients were ineligible if they were participating in an interventional study or the NIS CONFIDENCE (ML39632) or if they were receiving medication off-label, in particular off-label DMT. Procedures/assessments During the screening visit, eligible patients were classified into one of five predefined profiles based on their unmet medical needs. The five patient profiles were characterised as follows: Profile 1: Ongoing disease activity – patients showing evidence of disease activity (i.e., confirmed relapses, new/enlarged magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] lesions, or Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] progression) despite DMT. Procedures/assessments During the screening visit, eligible patients were classified into one of five predefined profiles based on their unmet medical needs. The five patient profiles were characterised as follows: Profile 1: Ongoing disease activity – patients showing evidence of disease activity (i.e., confirmed relapses, new/enlarged magnetic resonance imaging [MRI] lesions, or Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDSS] progression) despite DMT. Profile 2: Significant ADRs – patients experiencing significant ADRs or negative safety/tolerability issues with DMT. Profile 3: Low treatment satisfaction – patients reporting low satisfaction with their current therapy (i.e., low scores on Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire for Medication [TSQM]). Profile 4: Treatment-naïve – patients who have RMS but have never received a DMT. Profile 5: Not on treatment – patients with RMS who were previously treated or eligible for treatment but were not on any DMT at the time of enrolment. This manuscript focuses on the three profiles of patients who were receiving DMT at baseline (Profiles 1–3) (Fig. ). Results for patients who were treatment-naïve or not on treatment (Profiles 4 and 5) will be reported separately. If a patient met the criteria for more than one profile, an order of priority was applied: Profile 1 (ongoing disease activity) was given the highest priority, then Profile 2 (significant ADRs), and then Profile 3 (low treatment satisfaction). For example, any patient with evidence of disease activity was classified to Profile 1, even if they had significant ADRs or low treatment satisfaction. Similarly, a patient with significant ADRs was assigned to Profile 2 unless they met the criteria for Profile 1. Only patients with low treatment satisfaction (TSQM scores < 75.0) and without evidence of disease activity or significant ADRs were assigned to Profile 3. During the study, prospective assessments were collected through routine clinical evaluations and patient questionnaires at each visit. These assessments included treatment response (i.e., changes in disease activity and treatment type, including time to change), disease activity (i.e., confirmed relapse, disability progression, and MRI activity), PROs (i.e., changes in QoL, treatment satisfaction, and fatigue), and safety events. Additionally, for patients in Profile 2, retrospective safety data on DMT-related ADRs and serious ADRs were collected from patient charts covering 12 months prior to study entry. This retrospective collection captured the nature, frequency, and severity of any ADRs or serious ADRs experienced on DMT before enrolment. All treatments and any changes in therapy during the study were made according to standard clinical practice at the treating physician’s discretion and in consultation with the patient. Outcome measures Primary outcome : The primary endpoint was the rate of insufficient response to therapy at 48 weeks. Insufficient response was defined as the occurrence of confirmed relapse, EDSS progression, MRI activity, or treatment change. Confirmed relapse was defined as the appearance of new or worsening neurological symptoms lasting ≥ 24 h (in the absence of an infection or fever), occurring at least 30 days after a previous relapse onset, and confirmed by the treating neurologist (e.g., by documented neurological examination changes or an increase in EDSS score). EDSS progression (disability progression) was defined as a sustained increase in EDSS score by ≥ 1.5 points if baseline EDSS was ≥ 0 and < 0.5, ≥ 1.0 point if baseline EDSS was ≥ 0.5 and ≤ 5.5, or ≥ 0.5 points if baseline EDSS was > 5.5. MRI activity was defined as one or more new T2 lesions or gadolinium (Gd) enhancing lesions on spinal or cerebral MRI compared to baseline. Treatment change was defined as the initiation of a new treatment or any change in DMT status (switch or discontinuation), excluding treatment changes made solely due to pregnancy or pregnancy planning. Secondary outcomes : Secondary endpoints included: Time to first confirmed relapse during the study; Percentage of patients who were relapse-free by the end of the study; Change from baseline in EDSS score (disability status); Percentage of patients who had a treatment change during the study, including the reasons for treatment changes; Types of DMTs used and their percentages over the course of the study; and Change from baseline in PROs as measured by Health-Related Quality of Life 14 [ ], MS Impact Scale-29 version 2 (MSIS-29 v2), TSQM version 1.4, and Fatigue Scale for Motor and Cognitive Functions (FSMC). Safety outcomes: Safety was evaluated by assessing the incidence and nature of adverse events (AEs). This included all AEs, serious adverse events (SAEs), AEs of special interest (pre-specified events of particular importance), special situation reports (such as pregnancy or drug misuse), and any reported pregnancies. All AEs were coded and summarized by system organ class and preferred

their percentages over the course of the study; and Change from baseline in PROs as measured by Health-Related Quality of Life 14 [ ], MS Impact Scale-29 version 2 (MSIS-29 v2), TSQM version 1.4, and Fatigue Scale for Motor and Cognitive Functions (FSMC). Safety outcomes: Safety was evaluated by assessing the incidence and nature of adverse events (AEs). This included all AEs, serious adverse events (SAEs), AEs of special interest (pre-specified events of particular importance), special situation reports (such as pregnancy or drug misuse), and any reported pregnancies. All AEs were coded and summarized by system organ class and preferred term using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities. Statistical analyses Based on an estimated rate of 35% of insufficient response to therapy by 48 weeks, a maximum of 1,215 patients (a limit of 243 per subgroup) were planned to be enrolled across a target of 100 centres in Germany. This sample size was chosen to provide precision of 6–10% for the binomially distributed primary endpoint, based on approximation to normal distribution and a pre-defined two-sided alpha level of 5%. Statistical analyses were carried out using SAS, Version 9.4. The analysis of this study was exploratory, and descriptive statistical methods were primarily used. Analyses were based on the number of available observations for each endpoint. Missing values were not imputed, with the exception of missing or incomplete start dates for AEs, start and end dates of DMTs, dates of first MS symptoms, and dates of MS diagnosis. Insufficient response to therapy at 48 weeks and the corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using Kaplan—Meier (KM) analysis. Patients who were event-free were censored at their last available assessment date. Patients who changed treatment due to pregnancy or pregnancy planning were considered as non-events but not censored at the time of treatment change. If a patient died during the study, the censoring date was the date of death. Secondary outcome measures were summarised descriptively by profile as well as by time point/visit. For continuous variables, descriptive summaries were provided for absolute values as well as for changes from baseline by visit. Absolute change from baseline for each post-baseline visit was modelled by a linear regression model. An exploratory analysis using a Cox regression model assessed the impact of potential indicators on the insufficient response to therapy rate for the overall MS population. Numerical factors were age (in years), time since diagnosis (in years), disability (as measured per EDSS at baseline), and number of previous MS therapies. Categorical factors were sex (male or female), cognitive problems (yes or no), and FSMC sum score at baseline (< 43 or ≥ 43). A post hoc exploratory analysis was performed to evaluate the duration of DMTs at baseline. Results Study population A total of 973 patients from 66 centres were enrolled across the five profiles. After excluding patients who did not meet the eligibility criteria, who were erroneously profiled, or who did not have at least one post-baseline assessment, the overall MS population consisted of 920 patients. Of these, 488 patients were receiving DMT at baseline and thus fell into Profile 1, 2, or 3. Specifically, Profile 1 (ongoing disease activity) included 246 patients, Profile 2 (significant ADRs) included 179 patients, and Profile 3 (low treatment satisfaction) included 63 patients. The most frequent ADRs were lymphopenia in 7.0% of patients, influenza-like illness in 6.5%, and flushing in 5.9%. Discussion Profile 1 (ongoing disease activity) In Profile 1, the high percentage of patients with ongoing disease activity across the observation period may be due to initial treatment with low/moderate efficacy DMTs and therefore represent the need for escalation to a higher efficacy treatment [ , ]. Consistent with this, the most frequently administered prior and current DMTs were either of low or moderate efficacy. Furthermore, the percentage of patients not receiving any DMT more than doubled from 5.3% at the start to 12.2% at the end of the study. It is striking that, although 41.6% of patients had an insufficient response to therapy, only 14.2% changed therapy and 4.5% changed therapy within 28 days, all of whom had received a category 1 – low efficacy DMT. A similar pattern of limited therapy switching was observed in another German real-world evidence study, in which most patients stayed on the same DMT category that they had started on [ ]. Guidelines indicate that if disease activity is not sufficiently controlled, timely switching to another DMT, preferably with higher efficacy, should not be delayed [ , ]. However, many patients in Profile 1 did not receive timely escalation to more effective therapies despite ongoing disease activity, indicating therapeutic inertia and that guideline-recommended escalation strategies may be delayed or inconsistently implemented in decentralised clinical practice in Germany. This is confirmed by the duplication of patients in Profile 1 without any DMT at study end reflecting either insufficient monitoring or lack of knowledge about therapeutic options and guidelines. Although the rate of SAEs was highest in Profile 1 (4.1%), PROs indicate that the main concern for patients in this profile was a lack of treatment effectiveness rather than side effects. This suggests physicians may prioritise perceived safety risks of higher efficacy DMTs over potential benefits, i.e., favouring less effective but better tolerated treatments, reinforcing therapeutic inertia in clinical practice. Other factors such as reimbursement-related considerations may also contribute to the limited therapy switching, but this remains speculative, as economic barriers were not investigated in this study. Although these findings reflect real-world practice in Germany and may not be generalisable to other healthcare systems, they highlight a clear unmet need for timely switching to more efficacious DMT in patients with ongoing disease activity. In line with ongoing disease activity, patients in Profile 1 were concomitantly affected by impaired QoL, physical and psychological impacts of MS, and fatigue, with median FSMC scores indicating moderate fatigue. An indicator for insufficient response to therapy was severe fatigue at baseline. Despite being one of the most common symptoms associated with MS, fatigue is often not diagnosed and left untreated [ ]. Early detection of severe fatigue could aid in the timely identification of patients at risk of insufficient response to therapy, thereby improving treatment outcomes and QoL [ ]. However, fatigue as an independent indicator of insufficient response should be interpreted with caution due to potential confounding by psychiatric symptoms, such as depression and anxiety. These are known to correlate with fatigue [ ], but they were not included as covariates in the analysis. This limitation is further underscored by the fact that 13.4% of patients in Profile 1 reported a history of psychiatric disorders, including 8.1% depression. Nevertheless, screening for fatigue using suitable instruments, such as the FSMC, should be performed regularly in routine clinical care, particularly in patients with ongoing disease activity after receiving DMT. This limitation is further underscored by the fact that 13.4% of patients in Profile 1 reported a history of psychiatric disorders, including 8.1% depression. Nevertheless, screening for fatigue using suitable instruments, such as the FSMC, should be performed regularly in routine clinical care, particularly in patients with ongoing disease activity after receiving DMT. Despite the evidence for ongoing disease activity and impaired QoL, EDSS scores remained stable, suggesting no worsening of disability. However, lower EDSS scores are of limited sensitivity in the detection of insidious clinical worsening associated with progression independent of relapse activity [ ]. Profile 2 (significant ADRs) Despite Profile 2 representing patients with significant ADRs, the percentage of AEs was similar to the other two profiles. Furthermore, the number of AEs (28.5%) and SAEs (2.8%) reported during the observation period were low compared to the ADR rates from 12 months prior to enrolment (ADRs in 40.9% of patients and serious ADRs in 5.9%). Fewer AEs during the study may partially be due to a switch to more effective therapies after enrolment. Most notably, the percentage of patients on interferon beta (category 1 – low efficacy) decreased from 30.2% prior to study start to 20.2% at the end. This suggests that significant ADRs may be better relieved or resolved by switching therapies, rather than stopping. In contrast, fewer AEs during the study may also reflect an increase in the percentage of patients not receiving any DMT, which increased from 2.8% prior to study start to 9.5% at the end. Drug safety profiles are an important factor when considering a change in DMT regarding tolerability, potential serious side effects, and family planning. However, observations from Profile 2 suggest that the burden of AEs may be less important to patients than ongoing disease activity, when they are considering a treatment change. The most common reason for treatment change was ongoing disease activity (5.0%), whereas safety concerns were a less frequent reason (1.7%). In turn, patients should be offered timely switches to more effective therapies, even if they have a history of significant side effects or ADRs, accompanied by meticulous management of any emergent AEs. Ongoing physician–patient communication is therefore essential to assess individuals’ preferences in addition to their needs, symptoms, disease burden, and other clinical evaluations when considering a change in DMT. Profile 3 (low treatment satisfaction) Patients in this profile were slightly older and had a longer history of disease, which may be indicative of a greater overall disease burden. Also common was a family history of MS, a disease history of psychiatric conditions such as anxiety and depression, as well as high fatigue at baseline. Comorbidities such as depression and anxiety can make it more difficult to effectively manage and cope with MS, especially when coupled with elevated fatigue. Interestingly, male sex was identified as an indicator for insufficient response to therapy at 48 weeks. Some studies show that men are more prone to be affected by more progressive MS subtypes and a worse prognosis than women [ – ]. However, the mechanisms behind sex-related differences remains unclear. Since MS is three times more prevalent in women, most MS research is focused on the female experience, diagnosis, and management of MS [ ]. Genetic studies are improving our understanding of sex-based differences in MS, raising the potential for more personalized treatment [ , ]. As expected, low treatment satisfaction (6.3%) was the most common reason for treatment change (17.5%). TSQM results further demonstrate that these patients were the most unsatisfied across the profiles, perhaps due to them having the highest subjective impairment in physical and psychological domains of the MSIS-29. Severe/moderate fatigue, as demonstrated by the FSMC results, may have further exacerbated low treatment satisfaction. Studies suggest that treatment satisfaction is positively influenced by the absence of behavioural and psychological symptoms, fatigue, and pain alongside the presence of stable disease [ – ]. MS treatment is centred on preventing relapses, MRI lesions, and EDSS progression [ ]. However, these may not adequately address the needs of patients such as those in Profile 3, who suffer from severe physical and psychological impacts. Patient-reported issues such as fatigue, mood, and perceived disease burden should inform treatment decisions. Even with low detectable disease activity following treatment, many debilitating symptoms may remain. Patients with low treatment satisfaction require vigilant monitoring for subtle clinical changes, including emerging fatigue or cognitive/physical decline, using appropriate tools to detect “silent” disease activity. In their case, comprehensive care addressing symptoms and expectations is vital to improve satisfaction and adherence, even if conventional disease markers appear stable. Management of patients with RMS receiving DMTs Across the profiles, the most frequently used DMTs were low–moderate efficacy treatments (DGN S2k guideline: category 1) [ ], reflecting similar trends observed in other real-world studies [ , ]. Due to the heterogeneity of RMS and safety concerns with high efficacy DMTs, an “escalation” or “treat-to-target” approach is common in clinical practice [ , , ]. In these strategies, treatment is started with low or moderate efficacy DMTs and is switched on-demand to higher efficacy DMTs (e.g., sphingosine-1-phosphate -modulating drugs, cladribine, or antibody-based therapies such as natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, ublituximab, or alemtuzumab) if disease activity persists or reappears. This aligns with the DGN S2k treatment guidelines that recommend category 1 – low efficacy DMTs for patients with a low probability of highly active disease, and categories 2 – moderate efficacy and 3 – high efficacy DMTs for those with a high probability of developing highly active disease [ ]. Thus, high efficacy DMTs are usually used in later stages of therapy for patients with poor prognosis [ ]. On the other hand, the Association of British Neurologists guidelines recommend higher efficacy DMTs as the first option for eligible patients [ ]. Nowadays, growing evidence supports the early use of higher efficacy DMTs, through the “hit hard and early” approach [ – ]. Moreover, large retrospective studies demonstrate that the early use of higher versus lower efficacy DMTs is associated with a decreased risk of secondary progressive MS, slower EDSS progression, and less long-term disability [ – ]. Ongoing prospective randomised trials (DELIVER-MS and TREAT-MS) will help refine treatment guidelines [ , ]. With this in mind, a lack of translating clinical guidance to real-world practice is evident in the low number of patients on highly active DMTs observed in the present study. Limitations The 12-month observational period may not reflect long-term outcomes. The sample size was lower than planned (920 patients from 66 centres instead of 1,215 patients from 100 centres) and differed between profiles. Due to the low number of patients with rSPMS ( n = 18), data were pooled and interpreted for the whole RMS population. Profile 1 was the first fully recruited profile. This may reflect a high percentage of patients with ongoing disease activity in the real-world RMS population. In contrast, this may be due to the study design, with Profile 1 (ongoing disease activity) being of highest priority, followed by Profile 2 (significant ADRs) and Profile 3 (low treatment satisfaction). Despite the sample size, baseline characteristics such as age, EDSS score, and sex ratio correspond to other real-world RMS populations [ , ]. Nonetheless, a limitation of this study is the hierarchical assignment of patients to profiles, with Profile 1 prioritised over Profiles 2 and 3. As a result, Profile 1 may include patients who also experienced ADRs or low treatment satisfaction, as reflected by the higher SAE rates than in Profile 2 and relatively low satisfaction with effectiveness. While Profile 1 may therefore more closely reflect real-world patient populations, in which ongoing disease activity coexists with safety concerns and satisfaction/dissatisfaction, Profiles 2 and 3 may be less representative as they do not include patients with ongoing disease activity. In particular, Profile 3 recruitment was challenging, suggesting that low treatment satisfaction is rarely an isolated phenomenon but often coincides with clinical activity or side effects. Assessments were not mandatory due to the NIS design, but data were collected consistently to avoid bias. However, data collection depended on local routine clinical practice (e.g., MRI follows-ups were not standardised), and analyses relied on available data. PRO data were limited and should be interpreted with caution. Regarding the primary endpoint, the inclusion of treatment change into the definition of insufficient response to therapy introduces a degree of heterogeneity and subjectivity, as it reflects physician and/or patient driven decision-making in addition to objective disease activity. The results of the primary endpoint should therefore be interpreted in the context of real-world effectiveness and unmet clinic needs. Finally, although an insufficient response to therapy can be evaluated within 12 months of treatment initiation, the median DMT duration across the profiles may limit conclusions regarding long-term effectiveness. Despite these limitations, the PROFILE study is one of the few studies systematically exploring a spectrum of unmet patient needs in RMS, providing interesting initial insights into the challenges of different patient profiles in real-world care. Conclusions Following our approach, patient profiling in RMS across patient-centred and clinical dimensions (including traditional registry metrics such as relapses, MRI activity, and EDSS) adds actionable insights to enhance routine care. By incorporating outcomes like treatment satisfaction, fatigue burden, and perceived QoL, the patient profiles capture drivers of adherence, switching, and longer-term prognosis that may be under‑represented in conventional datasets. In this 12-month real-world study, our approach characterised unmet needs across profiles; over extended horizons, patient profiles may profoundly inform monitoring strategies, treatment decisions and improve patient care by supporting engagement with therapy, timely escalation, and supportive interventions. Accordingly, systematic profiling that integrates assessment of objective disease activity with PROs should become a standard lens for monitoring and decision-making, guiding both earlier use of sufficiently efficacious DMTs and targeted symptom management. Future work should validate these profiles over longer follow-up periods and across registries to confirm their prognostic value and refine individualised patient care pathways.
